The aircraft is powered by two high-bypass-ratio engines with a nominal thrust of about 35,000 lbf.
The aircraft is designed to carry 150 passengers at a cruise speed of Mach 0.8 over a range of 3000 n mi and to operate on a 6000-ft runway.

The design optimization used a multioptimizer cascade algorithm that employed sequential linear programming, sequential quadratic programming, the method of feasible directions, and then sequential quadratic programming again.
The regression-method-based analyzer exhibited a smoother convergence pattern than the FLOPS code.
The optimum weight obtained by the approximation technique differed by only 1.3% from the FLOPS code.
The prediction by the approximation technique exhibited no error for the aircraft wing area and turbine entry temperature, whereas it was within 2% for most other parameters.
The regression method had a tendency to hug the data points, while the neural network exhibited a propensity to follow a mean path.
The regression training required a fraction of a CPU second, while the neural network training took between 1 and 9 minutes.
For a single analysis cycle, the 3-second CPU time required by the FLOPS code was reduced to milliseconds by the approximators.
For design calculations, the time with the FLOPS code was 34 minutes, which was reduced to 2 seconds with the regression method and 4 minutes with the neural network technique.
The redundancy ratio (defined as the number of input-output pairs to the number of unknown coefficients) was 14 for the small model, 28 for the standard model, and 57 for the large model.
The performance of the regression and neural network methods was considered adequate and at about the same level for small, standard, and large models with the different redundancy ratios.
